blocks.text: Machine learning mechanisms describe how systems learn from data. Different mechanisms suit different problems: some use labelled data, some do not, and some learn through feedback and experience (Fig 6.4). Choosing the right mechanism matters, because the quality of learning depends on it.

blocks.title: Labelled and unlabelled data
blocks.text: Labelled data comes with the correct output for each item (a picture marked 'apple'); unlabelled data has no such answers.

blocks.caption: Machine learning mechanisms
rows: From labelled data: each input has a correct output, and the model compares its answer with it. It needs large, good-quality labelled datasets and is used for prediction (classification and regression).
Spam or not spam; cat or dog; normal or abnormal scans; face and speech recognition; fraud detection; exam result prediction
From unlabelled data: no correct output is given; it finds hidden structure by grouping similar items into clusters.
Customer grouping; data clustering; exploring data
By trial and error, like a person: an agent acts in an environment and receives rewards or penalties, aiming to maximise the reward.
A robot learning a maze; AlphaGo improving at Go; a self-driving car's decisions; recommendations adjusted by feedback

blocks.alt: Three panels. Supervised (labelled): three fruit outlines each joined to a label, apple, banana and grapes; each example has the right answer. Unsupervised (unlabelled): dots that form three coloured clusters; no answers are given and the system finds groups. Reinforcement: an agent box sends an action to an environment box, which returns a reward or penalty; it learns by trial and error.
blocks.caption: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning (original diagram after Fig 6.4).
blocks.long_description: Supervised learning needs a teacher's answers, unsupervised learning finds its own groups, and reinforcement learning learns from the consequences of its own actions.

blocks.title: Rule-based systems
blocks.text: The exercise also mentions rule-based learning, which the chapter does not describe. Rule-based systems follow if-then rules written by people, like the traditional programming in 6.3, so they do not learn patterns from data by themselves.

blocks.prompt: Which mechanism fits each task? (a) Grouping shoppers by buying habits with no categories given. (b) Predicting house prices from past sales. (c) Teaching a game-playing program by rewarding wins.
blocks.explanation: (a) Unsupervised (clustering). (b) Supervised (the past prices are labels; this is regression). (c) Reinforcement (rewards and penalties).

items: Reinforcement: rewards and penalties, trial and error.
